items.value: EIA WPSR price effect: absorbed within the [-5,+10] minute window; 5-min and 30-min windows give very close estimates
items.detail: Alquist, Ellwanger and Jin (2020), Bank of Canada SWP 2020-8. Announcement-day 15-min [-5,+10] return std 91.4 bp vs 39.8 bp non-announcement; -56.56 bp per 1 SD crude surprise (E.28). Absorption: the authors chose the +10-min window as sufficient for incorporation, and report estimates for 5-min and 30-min windows 'very close' to the 15-min benchmark (robustness tables for asset responses instrumented by oil returns). Reading: absorbed within about 5-10 minutes; no documented continuation to 30 minutes in this study.
items.quote: this interval allows for sufficient time for the news to be incorporated in oil futures and other asset prices | the point estimates for the shorter and longer window sizes are very close to the benchmark results.

items.detail: Baltussen, Da, Lammers and Martens (2021, JFE 142) Table B3/A3 via E.20 (E1). Peer-reviewed; horizon 30 min (last half-hour); out-of-sample R2 negative over the full sample (a null); gross. Shared source owned by EquityReader (F2_shared_baltussen.json); not re-read here.

items.value: positive in sample, gross: EIA-day third half-hour return predicts last half-hour (USO)
items.detail: Wen, Indriawan, Lien and Xu (2023), Energy Journal 44(5):149-171, accepted version. Underlying WTI via the USO ETF (NYSE hours), not CME futures. Horizon 30 min (hold last half-hour). In sample, gross; no transaction costs found in the text; rolling 5-year coefficient declining, not observed 2014-2016 (E.20). Also non-EIA days: first half-hour and overnight return predict the last half-hour (E3, E4); placebo r3 on non-EIA days null (E5).
items.quote: days with EIA announcements, we can generate an even higher average return of 4.14% per annum and a Sharpe ratio

items.value: EIA effect adjusts slowly, completed only at the end of the trading day (USO)
items.detail: Wen et al. (2023) conclusion: on EIA days the price response is a slow adjustment to the close (drift beyond 5 minutes), on the USO ETF (same underlying, another venue); in sample; effect declining over time and absent in 2014-2016 (E.20 E2 decay note).
items.quote: we show that the adjustment process is rather slow and is only completed at the end of the trading day.

items.detail: Borgards, Czudaj and Van Hoang (2021), Resources Policy. Horizon up to about 1 hour; gross; 6.5-month crisis sample; abstract-level only (E.20 E9 secondary-only).
items.quote: Finally, we find that extreme overreactions during the Covid-19 pandemic provide a great potential for profitable trading returns, which can be exploited by traders.

items.detail: Haugom, Ouyang, Smith-Meyer, Stordal et al. (2025), Quantitative Finance. Brent on ICE (same asset, another benchmark and venue). Net of costs as claimed in the abstract; in or out of sample not verified. E.20 E10 secondary-only.
items.quote: even when accounting for realistic transaction costs and margin requirements, some of the proposed strategies can create consistent positive and significant CAPM alphas.

items.value: API and EIA crude-inventory surprises both move 15-minute CL returns; EIA effect about twice API's
items.detail: Ye and Karali (2015), AAEA poster (precursor of Energy Economics 2016). 15-minute windows 10:25-10:40 ET (EIA) and 16:25-16:40 ET (API). Coefficients on crude shock: API -0.134/-0.126, EIA -0.231/-0.247. Absorption beyond 15 minutes not tested. 11 of 50 EIA reports produced significant return jumps; only 1 jump in the API window.
items.quote: The impact of crude oil inventory surprises in EIA report is almost twice the impact of the surprise in API reports. | In total, 11 out of 50 EIA reports generated significant return jumps.

items.value: jump clustering at the former pit open (8:55-9:10 ET: 18 of 133 jumps) and pit close (14:10-14:40 ET: 13 of 133); 8 at the 18:00 Globex open
items.detail: Ye and Karali (2015). Volatility/jump effect only (no direction). Times as printed (EST). The NYMEX floor closed later (date not sourced here); after that the 9:00 ET and 14:30 ET marks remain the US day-session open and settlement time.
items.quote: The number of jumps during the opening (18) and closing (13) of floor trading are considerably high.

items.value: EIA response is immediate, effects last about 25 minutes, then the price reverts quickly
items.window: WTI futures around EIA reports (period not in abstract)
items.detail: Geman and Li, Journal of Energy Markets (E.20 gives 11(2), 2018; volume and year not shown on the IDEAS page), 'An analysis of intraday market response to crude oil inventory shocks'. Abstract only. Volatility and volume elevated about 25 minutes; price effect reverts quickly (reversal, not drift). Also a pre-release move 10:20-10:25 strategy (see T6 item 31).
items.quote: Market activity, in terms of price return, volatility and trading volume, responds to inventory shock very quickly, with the effects lasting for about twenty-five minutes. Our results suggest that a positive (negative) inventory shock will result in an immediate price decline (rise), while both kinds of shock increase volatility and trading volume; however, the price reverts quickly after the initial reaction.

items.value: EIA-day strategies: following the 10:20-10:25 ET move beats trading after the 10:30 release
items.window: WTI futures EIA days (period not in abstract)
items.detail: Geman and Li, Journal of Energy Markets (peer-reviewed). Event-day intraday strategy; horizon not stated in abstract; in or out of sample and costs not stated. Abstract only.
items.quote: we exhibit an even better strategy than the “natural” one of going long (short) after the announcement of a lower-than-expected inventory at 10:30, that is, an alternate strategy that follows the market move between 10:20 and 10:25.

items.value: WTI (NYMEX CL) about 81.6% mean information share vs ICE Brent (lower-bound mean 69.3%)
items.detail: Elder, Miao and Ramchander (2014), Energy Economics (CSU repository preprint). CL leads ICE Brent; robust to pit/non-pit sessions, news days, millisecond data; the 2008+ Brent-WTI spread did not diminish WTI's role. CL is the leader of its underlying and of the Brent pair.
items.quote: The mean information share for WTI, averaged over 1345 estimates of daily mean information share, is 81.6%. | show a mean lower bound of 69.3%.

items.value: WTI-Brent (CL vs ICE B): economic/location pair; intraday lead-lag (price discovery) at one-second frequency, WTI leads
items.detail: Members CL and ICE Brent (also NYMEX BZ). Type economic (location spread). Documented intraday price discovery/lead-lag measured on 1-second data; authors state oil futures fully reflect new information within minutes. Lead-lag horizon: seconds to minutes (not stated as a minute-level predictive lead). Mean-reversion of the location spread documented at daily/monthly frequency (item 34).
items.quote: Using data on the most active futures contracts measured at the one-second frequency, we find that WTI maintains a dominant role in price discovery relative to Brent | markets are very liquid, fully re‡ecting new information within minutes (pdftotext renders the fl ligature as ‡)

items.value: crack (HO vs CL) and location (Brent vs WTI) spreads mean-revert; legs cointegrated (daily/monthly data)
items.detail: Dempster, Medova and Tang (2006), Cambridge JBS WP 25/2006 (later published). Type economic. Horizon daily or longer; no intraday evidence. Separate search for intraday crack-spread cointegration or pairs trading found no study (searched_not_found).
items.quote: Both market spread processes are found to be mean-reverting, which implies that their two price legs are cointegrated.

items.quote: based upon the VWAP of accumulated calendar spread transactions occurring between 2:28 p.m. and 2:30 p.m. ET, the calendar spread settlement period | Calendar spread trades are common in WTI Contracts and many other futures contracts.

items.quote: the end-of-day settlement at 2:30 p.m. ET) were exceptional.

items.value: US macro releases (nonfarm payrolls, retail sales, others at 8:30 and 10:00 ET) cause oil-futures jumps; response 'very rapid'
items.detail: Elder, Miao and Ramchander (2013), Energy Journal 34(3):217-237 (CSU repository). More than 30% of nonfarm-payroll releases followed by jumps (23 of 72). Jump detection at 5-minute sampling. Speed: rapid (within the 5-minute sampling interval); no post-release drift reported.
items.quote: employment situation report plays a key role, with more than 30% of the announcements on the change in nonfarm payrolls followed by jumps in oil prices. | oil prices respond very rapidly to new economic data

items.value: null for crude oil: no out-of-sample intraday (30-min) predictability; inefficiency only in heating oil and natural gas
items.detail: Wang and Yang (2010), Energy Economics 32:496-503, 'Nonlinearity and intraday efficiency tests on energy futures markets'. Peer-reviewed; 30-minute horizon; out of sample; nonlinear models; data before 2010. Abstract only. Note: Jiang, Xie and Zhou (arXiv 1211.4686, saved) paraphrase it as finding WTI predictability; the abstract names only heating oil and natural gas, so the paraphrase conflicts.
items.quote: Overall, there is evidence for intraday market inefficiency of two of the four energy future markets (heating oil and natural gas), which exists particularly during the bull market condition but not during the bear market condition.

items.value: multi-asset futures incl. crude oil: intraday reversion at 2-16 min, weak trend persistence at 1 hour+; tiny out-of-sample R2 (0.55 bp and 0.020 bp)
items.detail: Safari and Schmidhuber (2025), Physica A (arXiv 2501.16772v2). Crude oil is one of 16 pooled markets (with natural gas, gold, soybeans, equity indices, 10-year rates, FX); results pooled, not per market. Horizons 2 minutes to 1 day. Out-of-sample R2 by 12-fold cross-validation. Gross of costs. Peer-reviewed.
items.quote: The linear/cubic coefficients have switched signs and are now in line with the pattern from daily data: weak trends tend to persist (b > 0), while strong trends tend to revert (c < 0). | The adjusted R-squared, reported here in basis points (0.01%), has been estimated out-of-sample by 12-fold cross-validation.

items.detail: Wen, Wang and Zhang (2021), Economic Modelling 96:209-219. Same asset class, another venue and benchmark (Shanghai SC, medium sour). Horizon: overnight to the day session. Economically significant in asset-allocation exercises; costs not stated in abstract. Abstract only.
items.quote: We find a strong intraday reversal effect rather than a conventional intraday momentum effect. Specifically, the previous night’s return can significantly predict the day’s return both in- and out-of-sample.

items.value: EIA crude-inventory shock does not predict nearby CL returns after the release (10:35-11:00 and 11:00-15:00 ET); it does predict returns in the 30 minutes and overnight before (leakage)
items.detail: Luo and Kang (Illinois Institute of Technology), 'A Closer Look at High-frequency Prices and Trading Activities', ACFR conference paper (working paper). Absorption: within the 10:30-10:35 interval; no drift from 10:35 to 15:00 ET. Pre-release predictability is conditional on the ex-post shock (not an ex-ante signal). Text from a Firecrawl directQuote extraction of the PDF (raw PDF blocked by Cloudflare).
items.quote: we find that the inventory shock has no power to explain the return in the subsequent period after announcement (10:35AM to 11:00AM Wednesday) as well as in the remaining period (11:00AM to 3:00PM Wednesday)

items.value: after positive EIA surprises CL over-reacts: average drop about 0.5%, half reversed four hours later
items.detail: Rousse and Sevi (2016), FEEM NDL2016-070 (Energy Journal 2019). Post-release movement over hours is a partial reversal, not a continuation (drift) of the initial move.
items.quote: days with positive surprises are characterized by a large average price drop of about 0.5% – traders take short positions as inventories are larger than expected – which is partly corrected in the hours following the news release. Four hours later, the drop is half as large, i.e. 0.25%.

items.value: announcement-day effect and pre-release anticipation at daily frequency (futures and options)
items.detail: Miao, Ramchander, Wang and Yang (2017 version), 'The Impact of Crude Oil Inventory Announcements on Prices: Evidence from Derivatives Markets' (CSU repository). Daily horizon only; no intraday absorption measure.
items.quote: We document evidence of a strong announcement day effect on both markets, and find prices to move in anticipation of the inventory surprise.

items.value: ICE Brent: inefficient on average at sampling under 10 minutes; efficiency at lower frequencies (up to 2 hours) improves over 2006-2021; costs not included
items.detail: Smith-Meyer, Haugom and Ewald (2025), International Review of Financial Analysis 105:104424 (open access). Efficiency measure (AMIM, autocorrelation-based), not a trading test; authors state transaction costs not included. Same asset (crude), another benchmark and venue.
items.quote: At very high sampling frequencies (less than 10 min), the market is on average inefficient. For lower sampling frequencies, efficiency in Brent oil futures generally improves over the examined sample period.
